views.name: pizza_orders_base
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  co.order_id AS order_id,
  co.customer_id AS customer_id,
  co.pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  co.exclusions AS exclusions,
  co.extras AS extras,
  co.order_time AS order_time
FROM pizza_customer_orders co
UNION ALL
SELECT
  cco.order_id AS order_id,
  cco.customer_id AS customer_id,
  cco.pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  cco.exclusions AS exclusions,
  cco.extras AS extras,
  cco.order_time AS order_time
FROM pizza_clean_customer_orders cco

params.description: A normalized, row-level union of customer pizza orders (one row per order_id) combining raw and cleaned source tables.
params.when_to_use: Inspecting or listing individual pizza orders at the order_id grain. | Joining order-level attributes (customer_id, pizza_id, exclusions, extras, order_time) to other one-row-per-order datasets. | Feeding order-level data into downstream reshapes, aggregations, or joins that require the canonical set of orders from both raw and cleaned sources.
params.when_not_to_use: Aggregating metrics by customer, pizza, time window, etc. without first re-aggregating — this view is row-level and not pre-aggregated; aggregating directly may be fine but be explicit about the aggregation keys. | Using this view as if it were one-row-per-customer or one-row-per-pizza. Its grain is order_id, so treating it as customer- or pizza-grain will produce mis-counts and double-counting. | Joining this view to tables with multiple rows per order (e.g., order_line_items, toppings lists) without re-aggregating the many-side first — doing so will multiply rows and incorrectly inflate counts/metrics. | Assuming de-duplication between the two source tables: UNION ALL is used, so duplicate order_id values present in both sources will appear twice and must be deduplicated upstream if that is incorrect for your use case.
params.output_schema: order_id: unique identifier for the order at the order-level grain — derived from pizza_customer_orders.order_id and pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_id | customer_id: identifier of the customer who placed the order — derived from pizza_customer_orders.customer_id and pizza_clean_customer_orders.customer_id | pizza_id: identifier of the pizza product ordered — derived from pizza_customer_orders.pizza_id and pizza_clean_customer_orders.pizza_id | exclusions: textual or encoded list of ingredients excluded on the pizza for that order — derived from pizza_customer_orders.exclusions and pizza_clean_customer_orders.exclusions | extras: textual or encoded list of extra ingredients added on the pizza for that order — derived from pizza_customer_orders.extras and pizza_clean_customer_orders.extras | order_time: timestamp or datetime when the order was placed — derived from pizza_customer_orders.order_time and pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_time
params.grounded_columns: pizza_customer_orders.order_id | pizza_customer_orders.customer_id | pizza_customer_orders.pizza_id | pizza_customer_orders.exclusions | pizza_customer_orders.extras | pizza_customer_orders.order_time | pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_id | pizza_clean_customer_orders.customer_id | pizza_clean_customer_orders.pizza_id | pizza_clean_customer_orders.exclusions | pizza_clean_customer_orders.extras | pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_time
params.metric: no derived aggregated metrics in this view; all outputs are passthrough columns at the order_id grain | If you need aggregated metrics, compute them on top of this view, e.g. orders_per_customer = COUNT(order_id) GROUP BY customer_id
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to one-row-per-customer or one-row-per-pizza dimension tables on customer_id or pizza_id respectively — safe because those dimensions must be ensured to be unique per key (e.g., customer_dim.customer_id, pizza_dim.pizza_id). Example: JOIN customer_dim ON pizza_orders_base.customer_id = customer_dim.customer_id is safe when customer_dim has one row per customer. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables like a toppings map or order_line_items (e.g., pizza_recipe_topping_map) without pre-aggregation — such joins will duplicate pizza_orders_base rows and inflate counts. If you need counts of toppings per order, aggregate the toppings table to order_id grain first, then join. | Be cautious joining to sibling reshape or join-style views that expand rows (e.g., pizza_orders_with_names) if they produce multiple rows per order_id; confirm their grain before joining. | If joining to datasets that originate from the same underlying raw sources, ensure you handle duplicates consistently because pizza_orders_base uses UNION ALL and may contain the same order_id from both sources; deduplicate by selecting DISTINCT order_id or by applying source precedence logic before joining.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_with_names instead when you need human-friendly names for customers or pizzas — that sibling likely performs joins to name dimensions and returns the same order-level grain but enriches with labels. | use pizza_recipe_topping_map when you need a normalized mapping of pizza recipes to toppings (many toppings per pizza) — that view is reshape/many-side and not appropriate if you require one-row-per-order without expanding by topping. | do not substitute this view with runner_trips_clean, runner_performance_rank, topping_catalog, trees_by_zip, income_by_zip, companies_funding_summary, companies_with_dates_industries, or covid_stats_latest_by_state — those siblings serve unrelated domains or different grains (e.g., aggregates, ranks, joins) and will not provide the canonical order-level rows this view contains.

views.description: Normalized base of customer orders combining raw and cleaned order tables. Use when analyzing orders with canonical order_time (as ISO text), keeping both raw and cleaned extras/exclusions and preserving ids for joins. | Use for: count orders by pizza/pizza_name over time; join orders to runner deliveries or extras/exclusions details; filter orders in a time window or by customer

views.name: pizza_recipe_topping_map
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  TRIM(value) AS topping_id_text,
  CASE WHEN TRIM(value) = '' THEN NULL ELSE CAST(TRIM(value) AS INTEGER) END AS topping_id
FROM (
  SELECT pizza_id,
    SUBSTR(recipes.toppings, start+1,
      INSTR(recipes.toppings || ',', ',') - start - 1
    ) AS value
  FROM (
    SELECT pizza_id, ',' || COALESCE(toppings, '') || ',' AS toppings
    FROM pizza_recipes
  ) AS recipes,
  (
    SELECT 0 AS start
    UNION ALL SELECT 1
    UNION ALL SELECT 2
    UNION ALL SELECT 3
    UNION ALL SELECT 4
    UNION ALL SELECT 5
    UNION ALL SELECT 6
    UNION ALL SELECT 7
    UNION ALL SELECT 8
    UNION ALL SELECT 9
    UNION ALL SELECT 10
    UNION ALL SELECT 11
    UNION ALL SELECT 12
    UNION ALL SELECT 13
    UNION ALL SELECT 14
    UNION ALL SELECT 15
    UNION ALL SELECT 16
    UNION ALL SELECT 17
    UNION ALL SELECT 18
    UNION ALL SELECT 19
    UNION ALL SELECT 20
  ) AS starts
)
WHERE topping_id_text IS NOT NULL AND topping_id_text != ''

params.description: Explodes comma-delimited toppings on pizza_recipes into one row per (pizza_id, topping_id) with both the raw text and parsed integer topping_id where possible.
params.when_to_use: List or count toppings for each pizza (one row per pizza-topping pair). | Join toppings to a topping catalog by integer ID (after casting) or by text. | Filter pizzas by presence/absence of a specific topping (by id or text). | Feed into aggregations that expect the pizza-topping grain (e.g., distinct topping counts per pizza).
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to many-row tables (e.g., orders) expecting aggregated measures: this view is at pizza-topping grain — joining to an orders table without aggregating orders first can multiply rows and produce inflated counts. | Using it where a single-row-per-pizza result is expected (e.g., pizza-level summary): aggregating back to pizza level is required, otherwise you will double-count pizzas when counting rows. | Assuming topping_id is always present: empty strings are converted to NULL; treating topping_id as non-nullable will silently drop/incorrectly attribute toppings. | Relying on position-based indexing beyond the provided starts 0..20: recipes with more than 21 toppings will be truncated, causing missing toppings silently.
params.output_schema: pizza_id: pizza_recipes.pizza_id — the pizza identifier from the source table (base key for recipe row). | topping_id_text: TRIM(value) derived from the exploded substring of recipes.toppings — the raw topping token text (trimmed). | topping_id: CASE WHEN TRIM(value) = '' THEN NULL ELSE CAST(TRIM(value) AS INTEGER) END — the topping token parsed to integer when the trimmed text is non-empty and castable; NULL for empty strings.
params.metric: topping_rows = COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY NULL) is not defined in the view; to count toppings per pizza use: COUNT(*) GROUP BY pizza_id on this view. | toppings_per_pizza(pizza_id) = COUNT(topping_id_text) FILTER (WHERE topping_id_text IS NOT NULL) GROUP BY pizza_id | distinct_topping_ids_per_pizza(pizza_id) = COUNT(DISTINCT topping_id) GROUP BY pizza_id  -- NULL topping_id values are excluded by COUNT(DISTINCT).
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to topping_catalog on topping_id — safe because topping_catalog is expected to be one-row-per-topping_id; joining on topping_id will not duplicate pizza-topping rows. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to pizza_orders_base on pizza_id AFTER aggregating orders to one row per pizza (e.g., sum or count) — safe if the orders side is reduced to one-row-per-pizza before joining, because pizza_recipe_topping_map is one row per topping, not per order. | do NOT join directly to pizza_orders_base (or any one-to-many table) on pizza_id without pre-aggregating the other table: that will multiply pizza-topping rows by the number of matching orders and cause inflated measures. | do NOT join to sibling AGG views (e.g., trees_by_zip) expecting aggregation alignment unless you ensure compatible grain — this view is at pizza_id x topping_id grain, so aggregate to pizza or topping level first if needed. | When enriching with textual topping metadata, prefer joining topping_catalog on topping_id if you want one-to-one enrichment; if topping_catalog only has a text key, join on topping_id_text but be aware of trimming/case differences.
params.comparison: use topping_catalog instead when you need canonical topping names or attributes — topping_catalog (JOIN) is likely keyed by topping_id and includes descriptive fields; pizza_recipe_topping_map only provides raw token text and parsed id. | use pizza_orders_with_names when you need order-level contextual information (customer/order) already joined to pizzas — pizza_recipe_topping_map does not contain order or customer data. | use pizza_orders_base when you need normalized order records — pizza_recipe_topping_map is a reshape of recipes, not orders. | this view differs from sibling JOIN-style views (e.g., topping_catalog) because it is a RE-SHAPE (exploded tokens) of a comma-delimited string and not a normalized, authoritative catalog or aggregated metric view.

views.description: Explodes pizza_recipes.toppings (comma-separated topping_id list) into one row per pizza_id x topping_id. Use when you need to join recipes to topping metadata or to aggregate toppings usage across pizzas. | Use for: list toppings for a given pizza; count how many pizzas include a given topping; join to pizza_toppings to get topping_name

views.name: pizza_orders_with_names
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.order_id AS order_id,
  p.customer_id AS customer_id,
  p.pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  pn.pizza_name AS pizza_name,
  p.exclusions AS exclusions,
  p.extras AS extras,
  p.order_time AS order_time
FROM pizza_orders_base p
LEFT JOIN pizza_names pn
  ON p.pizza_id = pn.pizza_id

params.description: Order-level pizza records enriched with the canonical pizza name — answers which pizza (by id and name) and customizations were ordered and when, at the order_id grain.
params.when_to_use: When you need one row per pizza order (order_id) with the pizza's canonical name included. | When reporting or exporting order-level details (order_id, customer_id, pizza_id, pizza_name, exclusions, extras, order_time). | When joining order-level data to shipment, billing, or customer detail tables where the join key is order_id or customer_id and you must preserve the order-level grain.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view to tables that are many-to-one into pizza_orders_base (e.g., a toppings list with multiple rows per pizza) without first aggregating the many-side — doing so will multiply order-level rows and overcount measures because pizza_orders_with_names is at order_id grain. | Using this view to compute aggregates that assume uniqueness on customer_id or pizza_id without grouping by order_id — aggregating directly on customer_id or pizza_id can produce miscounts if customers have multiple orders. | Using this view to represent recipe/topping-level information — it does not contain per-topping rows (use pizza_recipe_topping_map for topping-level detail). | Using this view to answer time-window cohort retention or runner performance questions — those require runner_trips_clean or runner_performance_rank which have different grains and metrics.
params.output_schema: order_id: unique identifier for the order row — derived directly from pizza_orders_base.order_id | customer_id: identifier for the customer who placed the order — derived directly from pizza_orders_base.customer_id | pizza_id: identifier for the pizza variant ordered (foreign key) — derived directly from pizza_orders_base.pizza_id | pizza_name: canonical display name for the pizza — derived from pizza_names.pizza_name joined on pizza_id | exclusions: textual or structured list of excluded ingredients for this order (customization) — derived directly from pizza_orders_base.exclusions | extras: textual or structured list of added ingredients for this order (customization) — derived directly from pizza_orders_base.extras | order_time: timestamp when the order was placed — derived directly from pizza_orders_base.order_time
params.grounded_columns: pizza_orders_base.order_id | pizza_orders_base.customer_id | pizza_orders_base.pizza_id | pizza_orders_base.exclusions | pizza_orders_base.extras | pizza_orders_base.order_time | pizza_names.pizza_id | pizza_names.pizza_name
params.metric: No aggregated metrics are defined in this view; all outputs are row-level attributes copied or looked up. If you create derived metrics, do so by aggregating order_id (e.g., orders_count = COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)) to preserve the order-level grain.
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE: Join to dimension tables that are 1-to-1 or many-to-1 on pizza_orders_base keys, for example: |  - Join to pizza_names on pizza_id — safe because pizza_names is expected to be one-row-per-pizza_id, so it will not duplicate pizza_orders_with_names rows. |  - Join to a customer dimension (customers) on customer_id — safe if customers has at most one row per customer_id; this will not duplicate measures. | DO NOT join without aggregation to the following kinds of tables/views because they are one-to-many relative to this view and will multiply rows/measures: |  - pizza_recipe_topping_map (one pizza_id/order_id can have many toppings) — joining directly will produce multiple rows per order_id and overcount any order-level measures; instead, pre-aggregate toppings to the order_id level (e.g., list_agg or counts per order_id) before joining. |  - Any raw toppings, extras, or event log tables that record multiple rows per order_id or per pizza_id — either aggregate them to order_id first or join using EXISTS/boolean flags to avoid row multiplication. | Guidance: When you need to combine order-level measures with many-side detail, choose one of: |  - Aggregate the many-side to order_id (e.g., toppings_count_per_order) and join the aggregated result to this view. |  - Keep the many-side separate and compute rollups in a query that groups by order_id after performing the join, being explicit about COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) if appropriate.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_base instead when you need the raw, normalized order rows without any enrichment (pizza_orders_base is the source of truth for order-level columns and has identical grain). | use pizza_recipe_topping_map when you need topping-level rows (per pizza_id or per recipe) rather than order-level rows — that view is reshaped to the topping grain. | use topping_catalog when you need canonical topping metadata (names, ids) for lookup, rather than pizza_names which provides pizza-level names. | use runner_trips_clean or runner_performance_rank for runner/delivery analyses — those siblings have different grains (trips/runners) and runner-specific metrics. | use aggregate or rank siblings (trees_by_zip, companies_funding_summary, covid_stats_latest_by_state) only when you need pre-aggregated summaries at geographic or entity levels — they are aggregated and thus not suitable for preserving order-level detail.

views.description: Denormalized orders joined to pizza_names to expose pizza_name for each order. Useful for reporting orders by pizza name and downstream grouping or ranking. | Use for: top-ordered pizza names; orders per pizza_name over time; filter orders for a specific pizza_name

views.name: runner_trips_clean
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id AS order_id,
  runner_id AS runner_id,
  pickup_time AS pickup_time,
  distance AS distance,
  duration AS duration,
  cancellation AS cancellation
FROM pizza_clean_runner_orders

params.description: Provides one-row-per-order canonical runner-related trip details (runner id, pickup time, distance, duration, cancellation flag) for cleaned runner orders.
params.when_to_use: Retrieve runner-level trip attributes for a specific order_id (e.g., which runner handled an order, when pickup occurred, how far/long the trip was). | Join order-level trip attributes into analytics at the order grain (one row per order) without changing aggregation. | Filtering or selecting cohorts of orders by runner, pickup_time, distance, duration, or cancellation status.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view into an event-level or item-level dataset (e.g., order line items or toppings) expecting safe metrics — doing so will cause row-multiplication and over-counting because those tables are one-to-many relative to order_id. | Using this view to compute aggregates that assume a different grain (e.g., per-runner totals) without re-aggregating by runner — treating these rows as already-aggregated by runner would be incorrect (grain mismatch). | Summing scala metrics from sibling/child tables without confirming uniqueness of order_id in those tables — if you join to a table that duplicates order_id, summed distance/duration or counts of orders will be silently inflated. | Using cancellation as a derived metric representing counts/percentages without counting distinct order_id when joined to other one-to-many tables — this produces mis-counts of cancellations.
params.output_schema: order_id: unique identifier for the order at the order grain — sourced from pizza_clean_runner_orders.order_id | runner_id: identifier of the runner assigned to or handling the order — sourced from pizza_clean_runner_orders.runner_id | pickup_time: timestamp when the runner picked up the order (order-level pickup event) — sourced from pizza_clean_runner_orders.pickup_time | distance: numeric measure of trip distance for this order (units as recorded in source) — sourced from pizza_clean_runner_orders.distance | duration: numeric measure of trip duration for this order (units as recorded in source, e.g., seconds/minutes) — sourced from pizza_clean_runner_orders.duration | cancellation: cancellation indicator for this order (boolean/flag as stored) — sourced from pizza_clean_runner_orders.cancellation
params.grounded_columns: pizza_clean_runner_orders.order_id | pizza_clean_runner_orders.runner_id | pizza_clean_runner_orders.pickup_time | pizza_clean_runner_orders.distance | pizza_clean_runner_orders.duration | pizza_clean_runner_orders.cancellation
params.metric: order_id = identity(pizza_clean_runner_orders.order_id) | runner_id = identity(pizza_clean_runner_orders.runner_id) | pickup_time = identity(pizza_clean_runner_orders.pickup_time) | distance = identity(pizza_clean_runner_orders.distance) | duration = identity(pizza_clean_runner_orders.duration) | cancellation = identity(pizza_clean_runner_orders.cancellation)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to order-level dimensions (e.g., pizza_orders_base) on order_id — safe because both views are at one-row-per-order, so measures (distance/duration) will not be duplicated. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to runner-level dimension tables keyed by runner_id (if those tables are one-row-per-runner) — safe because runner dimension is one-to-one for runner_id and will not duplicate order rows. | do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables (e.g., pizza_recipe_topping_map, order_line_items, or any reshape/agg that contains multiple rows per order_id) without first aggregating that table to order_id — doing so will multiply this view's rows and cause summed metrics like distance/duration or counts of cancellations to be inflated. | when joining to aggregated views, ensure the aggregation preserves one-row-per-order (or re-aggregate after the join). Example unsafe join: runner_trips_clean JOIN pizza_recipe_topping_map ON order_id (topping map is one-to-many) — this duplicates trips for each topping row. | safe pattern for computing per-runner totals: SELECT runner_id, COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders, SUM(distance) AS total_distance, SUM(duration) AS total_duration FROM runner_trips_clean GROUP BY runner_id — aggregate here at the intended grain rather than relying on downstream one-to-many joins.
params.comparison: use pizza_orders_base instead when you need the canonical full order record or fields beyond runner/trip-specific attributes — pizza_orders_base likely contains broader order-level attributes and may be the primary order record. | use runner_performance_rank instead when you need pre-computed runner performance rankings/aggregates — that view provides ranked/aggregated metrics rather than raw one-row-per-order trip details. | do not substitute pizza_recipe_topping_map for this view when you need trip metrics — pizza_recipe_topping_map is reshape (one-to-many) for toppings and does not contain runner trip measures; joining it directly would multiply rows and distort trip metrics.

views.description: Canonical numeric runner trips using pizza_clean_runner_orders. Use for analyses that need numeric distance and duration per order/runner and pickup_time. | Use for: average trip distance or duration per runner; join deliveries to orders to analyze delivery times; identify cancelled vs completed deliveries

views.name: runner_performance_rank
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  runner_id AS runner_id,
  COUNT(order_id) AS trips_count,
  AVG(duration) AS avg_duration,
  AVG(distance) AS avg_distance,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(duration) ASC) AS duration_rank,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(distance) ASC) AS distance_rank
FROM runner_trips_clean
WHERE cancellation IS NULL OR cancellation = ''
GROUP BY runner_id

params.description: Ranks runners by their average trip duration and average trip distance, reporting per-runner counts and averages.
params.when_to_use: Compare runners by average trip duration (lower is better) or average trip distance (lower is better) across all non-cancelled trips. | Produce a leaderboard of runners (one row per runner) including their total completed trip count and average metrics. | Feed a UI that shows runner performance summary (counts, average duration, average distance) and rank positions.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view directly to a trips-level table (one row per trip) when you expect trip-level detail — doing so will duplicate these per-runner aggregates and inflate metrics. | Using the ranks as stable cohort identifiers across changing data windows — RANK() is computed over the current underlying data and will change as trips are added/removed, so it is not a persistent cohort key. | Filtering after join by attributes from a many-to-one dimension without re-aggregating — if you join to a table that expands runners (e.g., multiple employment records per runner) and then filter, you will effectively alter the aggregation grain and produce silently-wrong counts/averages. | Using duration_rank or distance_rank to compare runners across different time slices without recomputing over the intended slice — the rank is computed over all rows returned by the view's WHERE and GROUP BY; restricting time must be applied before aggregation to get correct ranks for that period.
params.output_schema: runner_id: unique identifier for a runner; derived from runner_trips_clean.runner_id | trips_count: number of non-cancelled trips for this runner; derived from COUNT(order_id) in runner_trips_clean | avg_duration: average of duration across this runner's non-cancelled trips; derived from AVG(duration) in runner_trips_clean | avg_distance: average of distance across this runner's non-cancelled trips; derived from AVG(distance) in runner_trips_clean | duration_rank: rank of the runner when ordering by avg_duration ascending (1 = smallest average duration); derived from RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(duration) ASC) | distance_rank: rank of the runner when ordering by avg_distance ascending (1 = smallest average distance); derived from RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(distance) ASC)
params.metric: trips_count = COUNT(order_id) filtered by (cancellation IS NULL OR cancellation = '') grouped by runner_id | avg_duration = AVG(duration) filtered by (cancellation IS NULL OR cancellation = '') grouped by runner_id | avg_distance = AVG(distance) filtered by (cancellation IS NULL OR cancellation = '') grouped by runner_id | duration_rank = RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(duration) ASC) computed per runner over the set of runners returned by the GROUP BY and WHERE clause | distance_rank = RANK() OVER (ORDER BY AVG(distance) ASC) computed per runner over the set of runners returned by the GROUP BY and WHERE clause
params.composition: Safe: Join to a one-row-per-runner dimension (e.g., runner_profiles if it exists) on runner_id — safe because runner_performance_rank is one-row-per-runner so the join preserves cardinality and does not duplicate aggregated measures. | Safe: Join to other one-row-per-runner summary views on runner_id (provided those views are deduplicated to one row per runner) — safe for the same reason. | Not safe: Do NOT join directly to trips-level tables (including runner_trips_clean or any other table with multiple rows per runner) without re-aggregating the joined result back to runner level, because that would multiply rows per runner and wrongly inflate counts/averages. | Not safe: Do NOT join to any many-to-one/one-to-many view on runner_id (for example, employment_history where a runner can have multiple records) unless you first collapse that view to a single row per runner (e.g., by aggregation or selecting a canonical row). Otherwise trip aggregates here will be duplicated. | Guidance: If you need to filter or slice by attributes that exist only in a many-row sibling (e.g., filter by zip histories), apply that filter to runner_trips_clean before aggregation (recompute the aggregates for the filtered set) rather than joining this aggregated view and then filtering.
params.comparison: use runner_trips_clean (NORM) instead when you need trip-level detail, exact per-trip timestamps, or to compute alternative aggregations / time-windowed metrics — runner_trips_clean contains the raw rows used to produce these aggregates | use covid_stats_latest_by_state (RANK) only for examples of rank-window patterns; it is a sibling that shares the ranking pattern but differs in grain and domain — prefer runner_performance_rank when your grain is runner_id and metrics are trips_count / avg_duration / avg_distance | lack of sibling with same metrics: there is no sibling that computes time-windowed ranks or persistent cohorted ranks; if you need ranks within a particular period, derive aggregates from runner_trips_clean with an appropriate WHERE on timestamps rather than relying on this view's global aggregates.

views.description: Ranks runners by average duration and average distance with counts of trips. Exposes runner-level aggregates plus rank columns for top-K selection downstream. | Use for: who are the fastest runners by avg duration; top-K longest-distance runners; compare runner speed vs trips_count

views.name: topping_catalog
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  topping_id AS topping_id,
  topping_name AS topping_name
FROM pizza_toppings

params.description: A canonical, one-row-per-topping lookup of topping identifiers and their human-readable names.
params.when_to_use: Enriching other tables (orders, recipes) by mapping topping_id to topping_name without changing row counts. | Populating UI dropdowns or reports that need a list of available toppings and their names. | Joining as a dimension to aggregate order or recipe metrics by topping_name (join only; do not expect aggregates here).
params.when_not_to_use: Joining directly to an orders table expecting aggregated order counts — this view is at the topping grain (topping_id) and contains no order metrics; joining to orders without handling multiplicity could produce incorrect aggregates (grain mismatch). | Using this view to compute counts, sums, or rates — it contains no aggregate measures; attempting to treat topping_name as a metric or to count distincts here to represent order volumes is a mis-count anti-pattern. | Joining to many-to-many mapping tables (e.g., recipe or order line items) and expecting this view to prevent duplication — since this is a dimension table, joining from it into a one-to-many table will expand rows on the many side and must be handled by aggregating post-join if you need de-duplicated measures.
params.output_schema: topping_id: unique identifier for a pizza topping; derived directly from pizza_toppings.topping_id | topping_name: human-readable name for the topping; derived directly from pizza_toppings.topping_name
params.composition: Safe: join to fact/order tables on topping_id (e.g., pizza_orders_base) — join to pizza_orders_base ON pizza_toppings.topping_id = pizza_orders_base.topping_id is safe from duplicating this view's rows because topping_catalog is one-row-per-topping; any duplication arises from the fact table side, not from this view. | Safe: join to recipe mapping when you only need the topping_name label for each mapping row — joining topping_catalog to pizza_recipe_topping_map ON topping_id simply enriches each mapping row with the name; it does not duplicate measures on the mapping side beyond the inherent multiplicity in the mapping. | Not safe without care: do NOT join topping_catalog to an orders-or-lines table and then sum a measure from topping_catalog (there are no measures here) expecting de-duplicated counts; the many side (orders/lines/recipes) will multiply rows and you must aggregate on the correct grain (e.g., SUM(order_amount) GROUP BY topping_id AFTER joining) or pre-aggregate the many-side before joining. | Not safe: do NOT perform a many-to-many merge between two one-to-many tables by using this view as the bridge and expect no row multiplication — this view is strictly a dimension; multiplicity depends on other sides of the join.
params.comparison: use pizza_recipe_topping_map instead when you need the relationship between recipes and toppings because that view contains the mapping (one-to-many) and possibly recipe identifiers; topping_catalog lacks mapping rows. | use pizza_orders_base instead when you need order-level or sales metrics per topping — pizza_orders_base contains normalized order/event data (metrics) and should be used (with aggregation) to compute counts/sums per topping. topping_catalog should only be used to supply names/labels for topping_id. | do not confuse with pizza_orders_with_names: that JOIN view likely enriches orders with names (including toppings) and contains order-level context; use that when you need order-level joins already resolved instead of starting from this topping dimension.

views.description: Simple pass-through of pizza_toppings to expose topping_id and topping_name for joins and lookups. | Use for: lookup topping_name by id; join toppings to recipes or extras/exclusions

views.name: trees_by_zip
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  zipcode AS zipcode,
  nta_name AS nta_name,
  boroname AS boroname,
  COUNT(*) AS tree_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Alive' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS alive_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status != 'Alive' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS non_alive_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN health = 'Good' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS health_good_count,
  AVG(tree_dbh) AS avg_tree_dbh
FROM trees
GROUP BY zipcode, nta_name, boroname

params.description: Aggregated counts and average diameter of trees by zipcode, NTA name, and borough (one row per zipcode / nta_name / boroname).
params.when_to_use: When you need counts of trees and simple health/status aggregates summarized at the zipcode × NTA × borough level. | When reporting tree density, proportion alive, or average trunk diameter (tree_dbh) for a geography defined by zipcode, NTA, and borough. | When joining a single-dimensional geography table (one row per zipcode or per NTA) to enrich these aggregated metrics without changing their totals.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to answer questions about individual trees (e.g., tree-level attributes or identifying a given tree) — the view is aggregated and loses row-level identity. | Do not use this view as if it were at a different grain (for example, per-address, per-street, or per-tree). Re-aggregating or filtering at a lower grain can produce silently incorrect metrics (mis-count) unless you re-run aggregation on the underlying trees table. | Do not join this view directly to a table that has many rows per zipcode/nta/boroname (for example, a permit table or resident table) without first aggregating that other table to the same grain — otherwise the tree counts and sums will be duplicated (aggregation multiplication) and produce wrong totals. | Do not treat non_alive_count as a separate base metric; it is computed as COUNT(*) - alive_count in this view’s SQL. If underlying status values change, counts must be recomputed from the trees table rather than adjusting derived columns externally.
params.output_schema: zipcode: postal zipcode used to group trees (source: trees.zipcode) | nta_name: Neighborhood Tabulation Area name used to group trees (source: trees.nta_name) | boroname: borough name used to group trees (source: trees.boroname) | tree_count: total number of tree records in this zipcode × nta_name × boroname group (source: COUNT(*) on trees rows) | alive_count: number of trees in this group whose status = 'Alive' (source: SUM(CASE WHEN trees.status = 'Alive' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) | non_alive_count: number of trees in this group whose status != 'Alive' (source: SUM(CASE WHEN trees.status != 'Alive' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) | health_good_count: number of trees in this group whose health = 'Good' (source: SUM(CASE WHEN trees.health = 'Good' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)) | avg_tree_dbh: average of the tree_dbh values for trees in this group (source: AVG(trees.tree_dbh))
params.grounded_columns: trees.zipcode | trees.nta_name | trees.boroname | trees.status | trees.health | trees.tree_dbh
params.metric: tree_count = COUNT(*) | alive_count = SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Alive' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) | non_alive_count = SUM(CASE WHEN status != 'Alive' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) | health_good_count = SUM(CASE WHEN health = 'Good' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) | avg_tree_dbh = AVG(tree_dbh)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a one-row-per-zipcode reference/dimension (for example, a zipcode lookup table) ON zipcode — safe because this view already has at most one row per zipcode/nta_name/boroname combination, and a one-to-one or many-to-one (this view -> dim) join will not duplicate its measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a one-row-per-nta_name dimension ON nta_name — safe for the same reason above. | Do NOT join this view directly to any table or view that is one-to-many from zipcode/nta_name/boroname (for example, resident lists, building permits, addresses, or any transactional table keyed by address) without first aggregating that other table to the same grain (zipcode, nta_name, boroname). Joining without re-aggregation will multiply tree_count and other aggregated measures, producing incorrect totals. | If you must combine this view with another aggregated dataset that is at a different geography (e.g., zipcode-only or borough-only), explicitly re-aggregate or disaggregate appropriately: either roll this view up (SUM tree_count, SUM alive_count, weighted avg for avg_tree_dbh using tree_count as weight) to match the other grain, or aggregate the other dataset to zipcode × nta_name × boroname before joining. | Do NOT attempt to compute ratios by joining a non-aggregated table and then dividing without re-aggregation first — this causes cohort/aggregation mismatches and mis-counts.
params.comparison: use income_by_zip (JOIN) instead when your primary question is about income by zipcode rather than tree counts — income_by_zip is designed for economic metrics and likely joins to income-specific sources and dimensions. | use companies_funding_summary (AGG) when you need company-level aggregated funding metrics; it is an aggregation view on a different domain and grain (companies) so it is not a substitute for tree-level or geography-level tree metrics. | the sibling runner_trips_clean (NORM) or runner_performance_rank (RANK) are in a different domain (runner trips) and should be used for trip/performance analyses; they cannot replace this view's tree aggregates. | there are no sibling views that produce the same tree-by-geography aggregation; prefer this view when you need zipcode × nta_name × boroname tree metrics. If you need a different aggregation (e.g., by borough only or by NTA only), compute a roll-up from this view or re-aggregate from the trees base table to avoid losing precision in avg_tree_dbh weighting.

views.description: Aggregates tree counts and basic health/status breakdowns per zipcode and neighborhood (nta_name). Useful for demographic joins and spatial summaries. | Use for: tree density by zipcode; health status distribution across neighborhoods; join trees to income_trees by zipcode

views.name: income_by_zip
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  zipcode AS zipcode,
  Estimate_Total AS Estimate_Total,
  Margin_of_Error_Total AS Margin_of_Error_Total,
  Estimate_Median_income AS Estimate_Median_income,
  Margin_of_Error_Median_income AS Margin_of_Error_Median_income,
  Estimate_Mean_income AS Estimate_Mean_income,
  Margin_of_Error_Mean_income AS Margin_of_Error_Mean_income
FROM income_trees

params.description: Provides income statistics (counts and central tendency) aggregated at the zipcode level from the income_trees source.
params.when_to_use: When you need per-zipcode totals and summary income measures (total population/total count, median income, mean income) as provided by income_trees. | When joining zipcode-level attributes (e.g., demographics or geographic shapes keyed by zipcode) where you need one row per zipcode. | When building dashboards or tables that report zipcode-level income estimates and their margins of error.
params.when_not_to_use: Joining this view to person- or household-level tables and treating the results as additional rows — the view is already at zipcode grain and contains aggregated metrics; joining to lower-grain tables without re-aggregation will create duplicated measures. | Using this view to compute aggregated metrics for cohorts that are not zipcode-based (for example, city, county, or state) without first re-aggregating to that higher geographic grain — summing means/medians directly is incorrect. | Attempting to compute counts of individuals or households by subgroups within zipcode by joining to one-to-many tables (e.g., a households table keyed to zipcode) and not re-aggregating — this causes mis-counts because the zipcode-level totals are repeated per joined row. | Treating margin of error fields as additive across zipcodes — margins of error require statistical combination, not simple summation, so aggregating MOEs across rows without proper variance formulas will give silently wrong results.
params.output_schema: zipcode: zipcode identifier for the geographic area — derived directly from income_trees.zipcode | Estimate_Total: total estimate for the measure reported by income_trees (likely total population or count in the zipcode) — derived directly from income_trees.Estimate_Total | Margin_of_Error_Total: margin of error associated with Estimate_Total — derived directly from income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Total | Estimate_Median_income: estimated median income for the zipcode — derived directly from income_trees.Estimate_Median_income | Margin_of_Error_Median_income: margin of error for the median income estimate — derived directly from income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Median_income | Estimate_Mean_income: estimated mean (average) income for the zipcode — derived directly from income_trees.Estimate_Mean_income | Margin_of_Error_Mean_income: margin of error for the mean income estimate — derived directly from income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Mean_income
params.grounded_columns: income_trees.zipcode | income_trees.Estimate_Total | income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Total | income_trees.Estimate_Median_income | income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Median_income | income_trees.Estimate_Mean_income | income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Mean_income
params.metric: Estimate_Total = direct column income_trees.Estimate_Total (no aggregate in this view; this view exposes the base aggregated value per zipcode) | Margin_of_Error_Total = direct column income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Total | Estimate_Median_income = direct column income_trees.Estimate_Median_income | Margin_of_Error_Median_income = direct column income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Median_income | Estimate_Mean_income = direct column income_trees.Estimate_Mean_income | Margin_of_Error_Mean_income = direct column income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Mean_income
params.composition: Safe: join to a zipcode-dimension or geography table (for example, a view that is one row per zipcode keyed by zipcode) on zipcode — safe because income_by_zip is one-row-per-zipcode so measures are not multiplied. | Safe: join to tiled geometry or lookup tables that are one-to-one with zipcode on zipcode. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables keyed by zipcode (for example, households, persons, orders, or other microdata where multiple rows share the same zipcode) without re-aggregating those tables to zipcode first — doing so will duplicate the zipcode-level income estimates and margins of error, yielding inflated totals or incorrect ratios. | When combining with other zipcode-level aggregated metrics, prefer joining on zipcode only when both sides are aggregated to exactly one row per zipcode. If the other side is aggregated at a different zipcode definition (e.g., ZIP+4, postal delivery area), reconcile to the same zipcode grain first. | If you need city- or county-level results, first aggregate this view upward using appropriate weighted combinations (e.g., combine totals across zipcodes for population counts; compute mean/median with appropriate methods) rather than summing estimate columns naiveley — particularly for median and margin of error calculations which require special handling.
params.comparison: Use trees_by_zip instead when you need additional tree-specific aggregates (AGG) computed over the same zipcode grain — trees_by_zip is an aggregated view and may contain sums or derived metrics across trees that income_by_zip does not provide. | Do not use pizza_orders_base, pizza_recipe_topping_map, pizza_orders_with_names, runner_trips_clean, runner_performance_rank, topping_catalog, companies_funding_summary, companies_with_dates_industries, or covid_stats_latest_by_state as substitutes — those siblings either operate on different domains (pizza/orders, runners, companies, covid) or have different grains/aggregation logic. Choose them only when the question pertains to their respective domain and grain. | Use companies_funding_summary or other AGG sibling views when your question is about aggregated company funding metrics (they are aggregated to company or other grains) rather than zipcode income statistics.

views.description: Pass-through of income_trees table keyed by zipcode to join demographic income estimates to spatial datasets. | Use for: join income estimates to trees or other zipcode data; analyze median income vs tree counts

views.name: companies_funding_summary
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  company_id AS company_id,
  valuation AS valuation,
  funding AS funding,
  CASE WHEN funding IS NOT NULL AND valuation IS NOT NULL AND valuation > 0 THEN (CAST(funding AS REAL) / valuation) ELSE NULL END AS funding_to_valuation_ratio
FROM companies_funding

params.description: Per-company funding and valuation snapshot: for each company_id, returns valuation, funding, and the funding-to-valuation ratio.
params.when_to_use: When you need a single-row-per-company snapshot of that company's reported valuation and funding amounts. | When calculating per-company ratios that use the stored funding and valuation values (e.g., funding/valuation) without further aggregation. | As the numeric source when joining company-level financial metrics into dashboards, reports, or further aggregations at a higher level (but only after respecting cardinality/aggregation rules below).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to compute company-level totals by summing its rows when the intention is to count distinct funding events or rounds — this view already contains an asserted per-company funding and valuation value, not an event-level sum. Using SUM(company.funding) across this view will only be correct if each company row represents the amount you intend to sum. | Do not join this view directly to a one-to-many table (for example, a table of funding_rounds, employees, or products) without re-aggregating on the many-side first. Doing so will multiply the funding and valuation values and produce inflated metrics (aggregation duplication/measure multiplication). | Do not use this view when you need time-series or historical cohorts (valuation/funding over time) — this view is a snapshot keyed by company_id and contains no time grain. Using it for cohort analysis will lead to incorrect temporal conclusions. | Do not use this view to compute per-round or per-investor metrics (e.g., average amount per round) because it does not contain round-level detail; such calculations require the underlying event-level table.
params.output_schema: company_id: the company identifier (derived directly from companies_funding.company_id). This is the primary key / grain column for this view. | valuation: the company's valuation value (derived directly from companies_funding.valuation). NULL if unknown. | funding: the company's funding value (derived directly from companies_funding.funding). NULL if unknown. | funding_to_valuation_ratio: funding_to_valuation_ratio = funding / valuation when both funding and valuation are present and valuation > 0; NULL otherwise. Computed using a safe division expression (casts funding to REAL before division) as defined in the SQL.
params.metric: funding_to_valuation_ratio = CASE WHEN funding IS NOT NULL AND valuation IS NOT NULL AND valuation > 0 THEN (CAST(funding AS REAL) / valuation) ELSE NULL END | valuation = valuation (passthrough from companies_funding.valuation) | funding = funding (passthrough from companies_funding.funding)
params.composition: Cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to dimension views/tables that are one-row-per-company on company_id (for example, companies_with_dates_industries) — safe because both sides are keyed at company_id and this view has exactly one row per company_id, so measures are not duplicated. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables such as funding_rounds (if such a table exists), employees, or other event-level tables on company_id without first aggregating the many-side to one row per company_id. Joining to a many-side will replicate this view's per-company funding/valuation values across multiple rows and cause measure multiplication (inflated sums/averages). | If you must combine with a one-to-many dataset, aggregate the many-side to the same company_id grain (e.g., SUM/COUNT per company_id) before joining. Alternatively, join first and then re-aggregate the combined result to a higher grain, ensuring you use appropriate aggregation functions (e.g., SUM of funding only if funding values are additive at the chosen grain). | When joining, prefer inner/left joins keyed on companies_funding.company_id = other.company_id. If the other side has multiple rows per company, use a DISTINCT/aggregation subquery to avoid duplication.
params.comparison: use companies_with_dates_industries instead when you need company-level metadata (dates, industry) alongside the metrics — it is a company-level join that contains additional attributes; prefer it when you need those attributes together with company metrics. | do not use trees_by_zip or income_by_zip — those are unrelated AGG/JOIN views with a different grain (zip) and cannot substitute for company-level financial metrics. | There is no sibling AGG view in the provided list that duplicates this company's funding snapshot; use this view specifically when you require the canonical funding and valuation fields from companies_funding. If you need normalized or cleaned company identifiers/names, join to companies_with_dates_industries (one-to-one) rather than replacing this view.

views.description: Company-level funding summary exposing valuation and funding amounts with indicators. Use to join to dates/industries and to rank companies by funding or valuation. | Use for: rank companies by funding or valuation; compute funding share relative to valuation; join funding to company founding year or industry

views.name: companies_with_dates_industries
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  d.company_id AS company_id,
  d.date_joined AS date_joined,
  d.year_founded AS year_founded,
  i.industry AS industry
FROM companies_dates d
LEFT JOIN companies_industries i
  ON d.company_id = i.company_id

params.description: Provides one-row-per-company details combining company date fields with a single industry string (if any).
params.when_to_use: Look up a company's date_joined and year_founded alongside its industry for reporting or filtering at the company level. | Build company-level cohorts by date_joined or year_founded while optionally showing industry. | Join company-level attributes into other company-grain analyses where industry is an attribute (not a measure).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to compute aggregate measures that assume one industry per company when companies can have multiple industry rows in companies_industries — it may silently drop or duplicate industry context depending on upstream data. | Do not use this view to count distinct industry affiliations per company or to compute industry-level aggregates without first handling possible many-to-one relationships; counting rows from this view equals counting rows in companies_dates, not unique industry affiliations. | Do not use this view as a pre-aggregated source for measures if you then join to other one-to-many tables (e.g., funding rounds) without re-aggregation — joins to such tables will multiply company rows and inflate measures.
params.output_schema: company_id: company identifier — derived from companies_dates.company_id (aliased d.company_id). This is the grain of the view (one row per company_id as present in companies_dates). | date_joined: date the company joined — derived from companies_dates.date_joined (aliased d.date_joined). | year_founded: year the company was founded — derived from companies_dates.year_founded (aliased d.year_founded). | industry: industry label associated with the company — derived from companies_industries.industry (aliased i.industry). Because the SQL LEFT JOIN does not aggregate, if companies_industries contains multiple rows per company this view will return multiple rows per company (one per industry).
params.metric: This view exposes no aggregated metrics. All columns are pass-through base columns from underlying tables. | If you need a metric, compute it explicitly after ensuring correct grain, e.g.: company_industry_count = COUNT(companies_industries.industry) GROUP BY companies_dates.company_id (aggregate on companies_industries before joining to avoid row multiplication).
params.composition: Safe to join: join to company-dimension or one-row-per-company views/tables on company_id (e.g., a canonical companies table) — safe because this view's effective grain is company_id as present in companies_dates when companies_industries has at most one matching row per company. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables (e.g., funding rounds, orders, trips) without re-aggregating those tables to company-level first — joining to a one-to-many will multiply rows and any counts/sums derived from the joined result will be inflated. | If companies_industries contains multiple rows per company, this view is effectively one-row-per-(company,industry). In that case, treat it as a one-to-many source when composing: re-aggregate industries to one row per company (for example, choose primary industry or array_agg/STRING_AGG) before joining to other company-level measures to preserve cardinality-safety. | When merging with measures (sums/counts) from sibling aggregate views (e.g., companies_funding_summary), join funding summary (one row per company) to an industry-aggregated version of this view (one row per company) to avoid duplicating funding amounts for multiple industry rows.
params.comparison: use companies_funding_summary instead when you need pre-aggregated funding metrics at the company level — companies_with_dates_industries is not aggregated and will duplicate funding metrics if joined to raw funding rows. | use a distinct/aggregated industry view (not provided here) when you need a single authoritative industry per company (e.g., primary industry) — companies_with_dates_industries returns whatever rows exist in companies_industries and may produce multiple rows per company. | This view differs from JOIN-style siblings like topping_catalog or pizza_orders_with_names in that it performs a simple LEFT JOIN without aggregation or enrichment; prefer those sibling JOIN views when you require name resolution or reshaping logic they implement.

views.description: Denormalized company-level attributes by joining companies_dates and companies_industries. Keeps company_id and exposes year_founded and industry for segmentation. | Use for: filter companies by industry and founding year; join to funding summary to analyze investors by industry

views.name: covid_stats_latest_by_state
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  state AS state,
  date AS date,
  total_cases AS total_cases,
  total_deaths AS total_deaths,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY date DESC) AS date_rank
FROM statistics

params.description: For each US state and date, returns the raw cumulative COVID totals and a descending date rank per state (1 = latest date for that state).
params.when_to_use: Find the latest (most recent) row(s) per state by filtering date_rank = 1 | Display or export per-state time series rows with an ordinal rank of recency within each state | Join state-level daily totals to state dimension tables when you need one row per state-date
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to produce aggregated national totals (e.g., SUM(total_cases) across states) without verifying whether 'state' contains non-overlapping partitions — aggregating across states is valid but ensure you intend to aggregate a per-state metric rather than reading a pre-aggregated national metric. | Do not use this view as a source of normalized rates (per-capita, percent changes, moving averages). It contains raw cumulative counts; deriving rates requires additional population or windowing logic. | Do not join this view to a one-to-many detail table (e.g., daily testing events, county-level rows) without re-aggregating the detail first. Joining directly would multiply rows and silently inflate totals (grain mismatch / duplication). | Do not reuse the date_rank column as a cohort identifier across different grains (e.g., county or facility) — date_rank is computed per state and date only; applying it outside that grain yields incorrect cohorts.
params.output_schema: state: US state identifier as provided in statistics.state — the partition key for the date_rank window | date: observation date as provided in statistics.date — the ordering key used to compute date_rank | total_cases: cumulative confirmed cases for that state/date as provided in statistics.total_cases | total_deaths: cumulative confirmed deaths for that state/date as provided in statistics.total_deaths | date_rank: integer rank generated by RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY statistics.state ORDER BY statistics.date DESC) where 1 is the most recent date per state
params.metric: total_cases = statistics.total_cases (raw cumulative count; not an aggregate) | total_deaths = statistics.total_deaths (raw cumulative count; not an aggregate) | date_rank = RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY statistics.state ORDER BY statistics.date DESC) (window function producing 1 for the latest date per state; note RANK allows ties and can skip ranks on ties)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a state dimension (e.g., states_dim) on state = states_dim.state_code — safe because this view is one row per (state, date); enriching with one-row-per-state attributes does not duplicate measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to other one-row-per-(state,date) views or tables on (state, date) — safe because keys align exactly to this view's grain. | unsafe: do NOT join this view directly to a county-level or other one-to-many table keyed only by state (or by state and another finer key) because that will multiply the rows for each (state, date) and therefore duplicate total_cases/total_deaths unless you re-aggregate after the join. | unsafe: do NOT join to a transactions/events table (many rows per state/date) without first aggregating that table to the (state, date) grain; otherwise sums/metrics from this view will be inflated by the multiplicity of matching rows. | note on window function and joins: because date_rank is computed per state using only statistics, joining additional rows that duplicate the same (state, date) combination from other data sources will not change date_rank in this view — but such joins will produce duplicate output rows unless the join target is one-to-one on (state, date).
params.comparison: use runner_performance_rank(RANK) instead when you need ranked performance metrics for runner trips — it shares the RANK pattern but is for a different domain (trips) and a different grain (likely runner or trip). | use trees_by_zip(AGG) when you need aggregated measures at the zip level — that view provides pre-aggregation and is appropriate when consuming aggregated measures, whereas this view exposes raw per-state per-date counts. | use companies_funding_summary(AGG) when you want rollout-safe aggregated financial metrics — that sibling is pre-aggregated and avoids the per-row duplication risk that would occur if you joined this view to many-to-one funding details without re-aggregation. | do not substitute pizza_orders_base(NORM) or other pizza/runner/topping sibling views for this view — they operate on completely different tables and grains; select the view matching your domain and grain (state,date) before composing analyses.

views.description: Selects the latest statistics row per state by date, exposing totals and a date_rank to allow filtering to the most recent period per state. | Use for: get latest totals per state; trend analysis by selecting date_rank <= N; join latest stats to other state-level datasets
